raw_text:
Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a major, age-dependent risk factor for ischemic stroke [1]. In nonvalvular AF, most thrombi originate in the left atrial appendage (LAA), a trabeculated cul-de-sac with variable morphology, contractility, and flow; this observation provided the rationale for mechanical exclusion of the appendage [2]. Oral anticoagulation remains the standard therapy for stroke prevention, with warfarin and direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) providing substantial relative risk reduction [3-5]. However, lifelong anticoagulation is limited by major bleeding, frailty, renal dysfunction, drug interactions, adherence, and patient preference. Percutaneous LAA closure (LAAC) was therefore developed as a nonpharmacologic strategy that substitutes a one-time implant, followed by limited antithrombotic therapy, for indefinite anticoagulation in selected patients.

Preprocedural assessment is central to LAAC. LAA anatomy varies widely in ostial size, depth, number of lobes, and angulation; morphology has also been associated with thromboembolic risk [6]. Multidetector computed tomography and transesophageal echocardiography define landing-zone dimensions, exclude pre-existing thrombus, and help select device size [7]. The first dedicated percutaneous experience was with the PLAATO system, which demonstrated technical feasibility and early safety in high-risk AF patients [8]. Subsequent multicenter feasibility data supported the concept but also highlighted the need for improved deliverability, sealing, and procedural standardization [9].

The Watchman device produced the pivotal randomized evidence base. In PROTECT AF, LAAC was noninferior to warfarin for the composite of stroke, systemic embolism, and cardiovascular death, but early procedural complications—particularly pericardial effusion—were more frequent [10]. Operator experience and registry surveillance subsequently showed improving procedural safety [11]. Residual peri-device leak was common, although its clinical significance was initially uncertain [12]. The ASAP study extended experience to patients considered unsuitable for warfarin, using dual antiplatelet therapy after implantation and reporting stroke rates below those expected from baseline risk [13]. Longer follow-up of PROTECT AF suggested reductions in hemorrhagic stroke and cardiovascular mortality compared with warfarin [14]. PREVAIL confirmed improved procedural safety but had more nuanced efficacy findings because of low event rates [15]. Patient-level meta-analysis of PROTECT AF and PREVAIL supported LAAC as an alternative to warfarin, with fewer hemorrhagic strokes but a small excess of early procedure-related events [16]. Pooled analyses also demonstrated less long-term major bleeding after the initial postimplant antithrombotic period [17]. Five-year randomized outcomes reinforced the trade-off: similar prevention of ischemic events, fewer hemorrhagic events, and lower mortality signals with LAAC [18].

Important complications include pericardial effusion, device embolization, vascular injury, peri-device leak, and device-related thrombus (DRT). DRT occurs in a minority of patients but is associated with increased ischemic events, emphasizing the importance of surveillance imaging and individualized antithrombotic therapy [19]. Contemporary registries have shown high implant success and lower complication rates than early trials. In EWOLUTION, Watchman implantation was successful in most patients, many of whom had contraindications to oral anticoagulation [20], and 1-year outcomes supported real-world effectiveness across heterogeneous antithrombotic regimens [21]. The US NCDR LAAO Registry established large-scale postapproval monitoring and demonstrated that LAAC had become a reproducible procedure across broad practice settings [22]. Iterative device design has further improved safety: the Watchman FLX, evaluated in PINNACLE FLX, showed high closure success and low major adverse event rates [23]. The Amplatzer Amulet, with a lobe-and-disc design, was compared with Watchman in the randomized Amulet IDE trial and achieved noninferiority for safety and effectiveness, with more complete early anatomic closure but different complication profiles [24].

The most clinically relevant contemporary question is whether LAAC can compete with DOACs rather than warfarin. PRAGUE-17 randomized high-risk AF patients to LAAC or DOAC therapy and found LAAC noninferior for a composite of stroke, transient ischemic attack, systemic embolism, cardiovascular death, major bleeding, or procedure/device complications [25]. Four-year follow-up sustained noninferiority and suggested less nonprocedural bleeding with LAAC [26]. Other approaches include epicardial suture ligation with the LARIAT system [27] and plug-based occlusion with earlier Amplatzer devices [28]. Postimplant imaging, including CT, can detect leak, thrombus, and device position and may complement echocardiography in selected cases [29]. Current expert consensus frames LAAC as most appropriate for AF patients with elevated thromboembolic risk who have contraindications to long-term anticoagulation, recurrent bleeding, or compelling reasons to avoid indefinite therapy, while acknowledging that optimal patient selection, postimplant antithrombotic regimens, and management of leak or DRT remain active areas of research [30].
